shouldFix.title: fx7Intent is a 320-character prefix of the live 404-character v9 FX-7 intent, and the dropped sentence — the one that says what a failure means — survives nowhere in the artifact
shouldFix.finding: permission-truth-tables.v9's FX-7 intent is 404 characters and three sentences. The catalog carries 320 characters — an exact prefix, so the first two sentences are faithful — and drops the third: 'A single differing decision means a clock or an arrival order entered the ordering.' I searched the whole artifact for that sentence and it occurs nowhere. It is 83 characters and it is not decoration: the first two sentences say what to run and what to assert, and the third says what a violation proves, which is the reason the assert is worth making. Without it the catalog states a byte-comparison obligation with no statement of what a differing decision would mean. This is the same defect, in the same field name, in the same lane, that the FX-5 sibling was rejected for one cycle ago — CLAUDE-FX5-SF1 required fx5Intent to equal the live v9 intent at 543 characters, and the FX-5 v2 fold restored it. FX-7 v1 repeats it at 320 of 404.
shouldFix.whyItMatters: The catalog's whole contribution is carrying v9's class forward to a fixture author. A prefix that stops one sentence early looks complete — it ends on a full stop, after an assert — so nothing signals that anything was cut. The sibling lineage has already established both that this matters here and what the repair is.
shouldFix.whatWouldRepairIt: Carry the whole 404-character intent, as FX-5 v2 now carries its 543.

shouldFix.title: Four of the five perturbation strings are the catalog's own constructions rather than v9's words, and the decision to isolate five perturbations from one combined run is undisclosed
shouldFix.finding: I tested each perturbation string against the live intent. One is a contiguous substring — 'host clock stepped backwards'. The other four are not: 'host clock stepped forwards', 'host clock frozen', 'control-plane messages delayed within what the transport allows' and 'control-plane messages reordered within what the transport allows'. v9's sentence distributes its subjects — 'with the host clock stepped backwards, stepped forwards, frozen, and with control-plane messages delayed and reordered within what the transport allows' — so the catalog has to reconstruct the four, and the reconstructions are grammatically faithful. But they sit unmarked beside the one that is verbatim, with nothing distinguishing constructed text from quoted text. The second limb is the reading itself. v9 says to run the whole of FX-4 and FX-5 WITH those conditions, which reads naturally as one perturbed run carrying all five; the catalog isolates each as its own initial state and says nowhere that it took that reading. Isolating over-covers rather than under-covers, so the choice is defensible and probably right — but it is a choice, and the artifact presents five states as though five were plainly v9's count.
shouldFix.whyItMatters: This is the pattern the sibling FX-5 v2 handles well: it carries each of v9's three asserts as an exact substring under a named field, so a reader can tell quoted text from the catalog's own. Here a reader checking fidelity finds one string that matches and four that do not, with no explanation for the difference.
shouldFix.whatWouldRepairIt: Either quote v9's clause whole on each state and name the isolated condition in a separate field, or mark the four constructed strings as derived and add one sentence recording that the catalog isolates the five conditions rather than combining them, and why.

advisories.title: v9's two FX-7 asserts are present only inside the quoted intent, not extracted, and the class's proves and name are carried nowhere
advisories.detail: v9's FX-7 carries four fields. The catalog quotes intent, in part, and carries none of the other three. proves is "ENFORCEMENT (of DR-G09's forbidden-ordering rule)" — the sentence that ties this class to the gate this catalog names in namedGate — and it does not occur in the artifact. name is 'clock and delay immunity' and likewise does not occur. The two asserts, that journals are byte-identical to the unperturbed run modulo the timestamp DATA fields and that no decision differed, are present only as text inside the quoted intent rather than extracted into a named field. The FX-5 sibling shows the alternative on this same contract: it carries fx5Proves exactly and lists its three asserts under assertsNamedNotAuthored both at file level and on every state. Adopting that convention here would cost four strings.

advisories.title: No failsIf and no whatThisCloses block
advisories.detail: The artifact exposes none of its own claims to refutation and carries no closure block, so a reader cannot see in one place that acceptance would close nothing by itself and that OBL-FX-AUTHORING remains. It does name the obligation in purpose and doesNot, so a recording act has an identifier to attach to.

coordinatorSummary: REJECT at 0 blockers and 2 SHOULD-FIX. Eleven attacks run, three landed. Custody holds: subject 693d8e26 at 0444, 4298 bytes, unmoved and unedited; HEAD never left 5d5d778; file 08 equal to the subject's own pin; required-now 26 of 26. Six of six cited digests reproduce, including the FX-5 sibling at ea47fc7d that a parallel dispatch requires to stay put. This Claude 2 path was free, so the verdict is filed. Every item on your attack list is refuted, and the unauthored discipline is refuted mechanically rather than read: all five states carry journalBytes NOT-AUTHORED, clockStepSize and delayDuration are NOT-AUTHORED where they apply, no duration-shaped numeral occurs anywhere, and the only bare integers in the whole artifact are 1 and 26 — the version and required-now. Five 64-hex strings, all citations. The catalog also gets something right that is easy to miss: FX-7's assert is a comparison against an unperturbed run, so the class needs two journal sets, and whatIsNotAuthored lists both perturbed and unperturbed journal bytes rather than treating the baseline as free. Two findings, both fidelity to v9. First, fx7Intent carries 320 characters of a live 404-character intent. It is an exact prefix, so what is there is faithful, but the third sentence is dropped and occurs nowhere in the artifact: 'A single differing decision means a clock or an arrival order entered the ordering.' That sentence is what a violation proves, which is the reason the byte-comparison assert is worth making, and because the prefix ends on a full stop after an assert, nothing signals that anything was cut. This is the same defect in the same field name in the same lane that the FX-5 sibling was rejected for one cycle ago at 543 characters; I measured FX-7's independently rather than reasoning from that. Second, four of the five perturbation strings are the catalog's own constructions — only 'host clock stepped backwards' is a contiguous substring of v9 — and they sit unmarked beside the one that is verbatim; the related limb is that v9 says to run FX-4 and FX-5 WITH all five conditions, which reads as one combined run, while the catalog isolates five and records nowhere that it took that reading. Isolating over-covers and is probably the right call, so the defect is the silence, not the choice. Two advisories: v9's FX-7 also carries proves — "ENFORCEMENT (of DR-G09's forbidden-ordering rule)", the sentence tying this class to the gate the catalog names — and name, and neither occurs in the artifact, while the two asserts sit only inside the quoted intent rather than extracted, where the FX-5 sibling carries its proves exactly and its three asserts under a named field on every state; and there is no failsIf and no whatThisCloses. Both repairs are additive and neither touches the five states.
